summary: Describes how to use the GOST 28147-89, GOST R 34.10-94, GOST R 34.10-2001 and GOST R 34.11-94 cryptographic algorithms with the Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS), which is used for signing, hashing, authenticating and encrypting messages. It is a proposed standard.

eli5.summary: Explains how to use some Russian lock-and-signature methods in a common envelope format used for secure messages.

questions: using gost algorithms in cryptographic message syntax
how to use gost algorithms with cms
subtitle: How to plug four Russian GOST algorithms into the Cryptographic Message Syntax used for signed and encrypted messages.

tldr.problem: The Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS) can sign, hash, authenticate and encrypt messages, but it needs identifiers and field conventions for each algorithm. The Russian GOST algorithms had none.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC assigns object identifiers and says which CMS fields carry GOST R 34.11-94 digests, GOST R 34.10-94 and 34.10-2001 signatures, key agreement and key transport values, GOST 28147-89 encrypted content and HMAC values.
tldr.outcome: Implementations from the Russian Cryptographic Software Compatibility Agreement community can exchange GOST-protected CMS and S/MIME messages. The RFC is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted.

today: RFC 4490 is a Proposed Standard published in May 2006, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It remains the definition of how these four GOST algorithms are used in CMS.

sections.title: Introduction and Scope
sections.content:
The Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS, see RFC 3852) is used for digital signature, digest, authentication and encryption of arbitrary message contents. This RFC is a companion specification that describes how four cryptographic algorithms fit into it: GOST 28147-89, GOST R 34.10-94, GOST R 34.10-2001 and GOST R 34.11-94.

It was proposed by the CRYPTO-PRO Company for the "Russian Cryptographic Software Compatibility Agreement" community. The document does not describe the algorithms themselves. They are defined in national standards, and this RFC only says how to use them in CMS.

CMS values are generated with ASN.1 and encoded with BER. For each algorithm the RFC gives the algorithm identifier (an ASN.1 object identifier plus any parameters) and names the CMS fields the algorithm uses. Keywords such as MUST and SHOULD carry their RFC 2119 meaning.
sections.eli5: The algorithms are the locks. This document does not build the locks. It only says where on the envelope each lock and seal goes.

sections.title: Digest and Signature Algorithms
sections.content:
GOST R 34.11-94 is the hash function. It produces a 256-bit hash value from an input of any finite bit length. In CMS its identifier is id-GostR3411-94. The AlgorithmIdentifier parameters field MUST be present and MUST contain NULL, although implementations MAY also accept absent parameters. The function is always used with the default parameter set id-GostR3411-94-CryptoProParamSet. When the Message Digest authenticated attribute is present, the digest is a 32-byte value in little-endian form.

Digest values live in the DigestedData digest field and in the Message Digest authenticated attribute, and they are also the input to the signature algorithms.

Both signature algorithms, GOST R 34.10-94 and GOST R 34.10-2001, MUST be used together with GOST R 34.11-94. Each produces a signature made of two 256-bit numbers. The signature is written as an octet string of 64 octets: the first 32 octets hold the big-endian representation of s, and the second 32 hold the big-endian representation of r' (for the 1994 algorithm) or r (for the 2001 algorithm). Signature values go in the SignerInfo signature field, and the algorithm identifier goes in the signatureAlgorithm field, including inside countersignature attributes.
sections.eli5: The hash is a short fingerprint of a message, and the signature is a stamp made from that fingerprint. Both are put in fixed boxes on the envelope so the receiver knows where to look.

sections.title: Key Agreement and Key Transport
sections.content:
The key management algorithms are based on the VKO GOST R 34.10-94 and VKO GOST R 34.10-2001 key derivation algorithms and on the CryptoPro and GOST 28147-89 key wrap algorithms, which are described in RFC 4357. They MUST be used only with the GOST 28147-89 content encryption algorithm.

With key agreement, the KeyAgreeRecipientInfo version MUST be 3 and the originator MUST be the originatorKey alternative, holding the sender's public key. The keyEncryptionAlgorithm MUST be id-GostR3410-94-CryptoPro-ESDH or id-GostR3410-2001-CryptoPro-ESDH, depending on the recipient's public key, and its parameter names the key wrap algorithm. The ukm (user keying material) in KeyAgreeRecipientInfo MUST be present and contain eight octets. The sender's secret key and the recipient's public key produce a key encryption key (KEK), and the key wrap algorithm then yields the encrypted content key, its MAC and the UKM.

With key transport, the KeyTransRecipientInfo version MUST be 0 or 3, and the key encryption algorithm and parameters MUST be identical to the recipient's public key algorithm and parameters. The encrypted key holds a GostR3410-KeyTransport structure with the encrypted content key, its MAC, the GOST 28147-89 parameters used, the sender's ephemeral public key and the UKM. The transportParameters and ephemeralPublicKey MUST be present.
sections.eli5: To send a secret key to someone, you wrap it in a locked box that only they can open. This section says exactly how the box is built and which label goes on it.

sections.title: Content Encryption and MAC
sections.content:
GOST 28147-89 encrypts the message content, in both EnvelopedData and EncryptedData. Its identifier is id-Gost28147-89. The algorithm parameters MUST be present and consist of an 8-octet initialization vector (iv) and an encryptionParamSet object identifier that selects the parameter set.

For authentication, AuthenticatedData can use HMAC built on GOST R 34.11-94, named id-HMACGostR3411-94. It has the same parameters as the GOST R 34.11-94 digest algorithm and uses the same OIDs for them. The MAC algorithm identifier goes in the macAlgorithm field and the result in the mac field.
sections.eli5: The content is scrambled with a secret code before it goes in the envelope. A second seal proves nobody changed it on the way.

sections.title: Use with S/MIME
sections.content:
The algorithms can also be used with S/MIME (RFC 3851). When they are used, the micalg parameter SHOULD be set to gostr3411-94; otherwise it MUST be set to unknown.

The SMIMECapabilities attribute announces what a sender supports. A capability for the GOST R 34.11-94 digest carries the identifier id-GostR3411-94 with no parameters, and one for GOST 28147-89 carries id-Gost28147-89 with no parameters. The RFC gives the DER bytes for each. To advertise a specific parameter set, the capability MUST carry the Gost28147-89-Parameters structure. Recipients MUST ignore its iv field and assume the sender supports the parameter set in encryptionParamSet.
sections.eli5: Email programs can put a small note on a message saying which locks they understand. This section says how to write that note for the GOST locks.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Conforming applications MUST use unique values for ukm and iv. Recipients MAY check that the values a sender supplied are unique.

The RFC recommends that software verify that signature values, subject public keys and algorithm parameters conform to the GOST R 34.10-2001 and GOST R 34.10-94 standards before using them. Parameters affect algorithm strength, so parameters not listed in RFC 4357 are NOT RECOMMENDED. Using the same key for signing and for key derivation is also NOT RECOMMENDED.

When signed CMS documents are used as the analogue of a manual signature under the Russian Federal Electronic Digital Signature Law, the signer certificate MUST contain a critical keyUsage extension that does not include keyEncipherment or keyAgreement. Applications SHOULD be submitted for examination by an authorized agency.
sections.eli5: Never reuse the same one-time scramble number, and only use the settings the experts listed. Do not use one key for two different jobs.

sections.title: Examples and ASN.1 Modules
sections.content:
The RFC includes three sample messages built with the sample certificate from RFC 4491: a signed message, an enveloped message using key agreement and an enveloped message using key transport. Each is shown as a decoded ASN.1 dump and as a Base64 blob that can be extracted and decoded. They are stored in the same format as the examples in RFC 4134.

Section 10 gives ASN.1 modules for the encryption syntax and for the GOST R 34.10-94 and GOST R 34.10-2001 signature syntax. Further modules are referenced from RFC 4357.
sections.eli5: The document includes real sample envelopes, so people building software can check that their envelopes look exactly the same.

items.desc: Needs an 8-octet iv and a parameter set.
